plants.container: Light grey pot inside a darker grey bowl, bark mix, with a white plant marker and a hand-written tag
plants.id_basis: Upright fronds with tightly crimped, curled leaflets, the same as the 'Emina' Boston fern (P-024). This is a second pot: a light grey pot in a darker grey bowl, with its own hand-written tag that the photos do not show clearly.
plants.id_improve: A close photo of the tag
plants.temp_notes: Fronds are frost-tender; roots can survive a light freeze.
plants.humidity_notes: High humidity is the main requirement; dry air crisps fronds quickly.
plants.winter_summary: Needs humidity and a frost-free spot.
plants.winter_steps:
Target: indoors by about Nov 1, before the first night forecast under 50 F.
Pre-move: rinse the leaves with a hose, check undersides and stem nodes for spider mites, mealybugs, scale and fungus gnats, treat with insecticidal soap or neem, then quarantine 2 weeks away from other houseplants.
Acclimate in two steps to limit leaf drop: about a week on the covered porch or in the garage, then inside.
Do not repot or fertilize for the move; trim only dead tissue.
Cut all dead fronds to the base before moving so it can regrow clean.
plants.indoor_setup:
Indoor winter air is typically 20-35% RH; raise it with a humidifier (target 50-60%), grouping plants, or a pebble tray, and keep plants away from heater vents.
Indoors: within 3 ft of an east or south window, or under a full-spectrum grow light 12-14 h/day at 6-12 in. Winter sun in Round Rock is only ~4.5-6 hours of real sunshine per day in Dec-Jan, so supplement.
Keep the mix evenly moist like a wrung-out sponge.
plants.health_summary: Mostly dead, crisped fronds, but healthy new curly fronds are coming from the crown, as on P-024.
plants.health_observations:
Most old fronds dry, brown and crisped
A few green fronds, and one fresh bright-green curly frond
Spurge weed (red stems, small oval leaves) growing in the pot
Chunky bark mix
plants.health_steps:
Cut the dead fronds off at the base. Leave every green frond.
Pull the spurge weed. Wear gloves: its milky sap irritates skin.
Keep the mix evenly moist and never let it dry out completely; ferns die back when they dry out.
Bright light without afternoon sun.
Bring it in before nights fall below 40°F.
plants.notes: Second curly Boston fern, photographed on October 25, 2026.
plants.water_notes: Keep the mix consistently damp like a wrung-out sponge. A fern that dries out drops fronds quickly. Do not leave it standing in water.
plants.soil_medium: Rich, moisture-holding mix: potting soil with extra coir or peat, 20% perlite and a little compost.
plants.nutrients: Feed lightly about once a month in spring and summer at quarter strength. Ferns are easily burned by fertilizer. Pale fronds can mean too much light.
plants.pests_watch:
Scale and mealybugs on fronds and crown
Spider mites in dry air
Fungus gnats
Fungal leaf spot
Pesticide burn: ferns are easily damaged by oils and soaps
plants.pest_steps:
Look at the undersides of fronds and the crown weekly.
Treat scale or mealybugs by dabbing with a swab of 70% rubbing alcohol; avoid oils and soaps on ferns, or test on one frond first.
Keep the humidity up and the mix damp to discourage mites.
Cut off badly damaged fronds at the base.
plants.growth_habit: Evergreen fern, with arching fronds and running stolons
plants.zone_notes: Fronds are damaged by frost; roots can survive light freezes in the ground in zone 9b.
plants.native_range: Tropical and subtropical Americas, including Florida, Mexico, the Caribbean and northern South America, as well as parts of Africa and Polynesia. Boston fern is a selection of it.
plants.conservation_status: No IUCN Red List assessment that Claude could confirm.
plants.invasive: Its cousin, sword fern (Nephrolepis cordifolia), is invasive in Florida. Boston fern cultivars spread mostly in pots.
plants.bloom: None: ferns reproduce by spores, which are the brown dots under the fronds.
plants.danger_animals: Non-toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA lists Boston fern as non-toxic).
plants.propagation:
Division of the crown.
Pin down the runners (stolons) onto moist mix; each rooted tip becomes a new plant.

plants.container: Wide beige pot, chunky mix with perlite, bark and lava rock
plants.id_basis: Heart-shaped young leaves that already have holes near the midrib and notches at the edge, the way young Monstera deliciosa leaves begin. The shoots come up from an old knot of roots, so it is probably regrowing from a stem cutting or an older plant that was cut back.
plants.id_alternatives:
Monstera adansonii (thinner, longer leaves with many holes)
Epipremnum pinnatum (young leaves can also have holes)
Rhaphidophora tetrasperma ('mini monstera'; splits to the edge, no holes)

plants.temp_notes: Leaves are damaged below about 45 F. Frost kills them.
plants.humidity_notes: Tolerates average indoor humidity; the leaf edges dry out below about 35%.
plants.light_notes: Direct hot sun scorches the leaves. The tan or yellow margins on the front leaves may be sun, cold or dry air.
plants.winter_summary: Tropical climber. Bring it in before nights fall under 50 F.
plants.winter_triggers: Target Nov 1; before any night under 50 F.
plants.winter_steps:
Target: indoors by about Nov 1, before the first night forecast under 50 F.
Pre-move: rinse the leaves with a hose, check undersides and stem nodes for spider mites, mealybugs, scale and fungus gnats, treat with insecticidal soap or neem, then quarantine 2 weeks away from other houseplants.
Acclimate in two steps to limit leaf drop: about a week on the covered porch or in the garage, then inside.
Do not repot or fertilize for the move; trim only dead tissue.
plants.indoor_setup:
Indoors: within 3 ft of an east or south window, or under a full-spectrum grow light 12-14 h/day at 6-12 in. Winter sun in Round Rock is only ~4.5-6 hours of real sunshine per day in Dec-Jan, so supplement.
Indoor winter air is typically 20-35% RH; raise it with a humidifier (target 50-60%), grouping plants, or a pebble tray, and keep plants away from heater vents.
Water when the top 2 in of the mix are dry; reduce watering in winter.
Keep the pole damp to encourage aerial roots to grab it.
plants.health_summary: Several healthy young shoots with their first holes and notches. The leaves are pale and a little puckered, which is common for new growth in cool weather.
plants.health_observations:
Three or four young shoots from an old root knot
First holes and edge notches on the newest leaves
Pale, slightly puckered young leaves
Two or three tiny seedlings in the mix (probably weeds)
plants.health_steps:
Bring it in before nights fall below 50°F.
Keep the mix lightly moist, not wet, while it is small.
Bright light without direct afternoon sun.
Add a small moss pole or stake once a shoot starts to climb.
Pull the tiny seedlings unless you planted them.
plants.notes: Photographed on October 25, 2026, on the porch shelf.
plants.water_notes: Water when the top 1-2 in (3-5 cm) of mix is dry. Soak until water drains out, then empty the saucer. Indoors in winter this stretches to every 10-14 days. Cold, wet mix is the commonest way to lose these plants.
plants.soil_medium: Chunky, fast-draining aroid mix: about 40% potting soil, 30% orchid bark, 20% perlite or pumice and 10% coco coir or worm castings. The pot must have drainage holes.
plants.fertilizer: Balanced liquid, such as 3-1-2 or 20-20-20, at half strength
plants.nutrients: Feed every 2-4 weeks from March to September at half strength, and stop from November to February. Pale new leaves point to low nitrogen. Yellow older leaves with green veins point to low magnesium (1 tsp Epsom salt per gallon, once a season). Brown crisp tips can be salt build-up: flush the pot with plain water every 2-3 months.
plants.pests_watch:
Spider mites: fine webbing and stippled leaves, worst in dry heated air
Thrips: silvery streaks and black specks on leaves
Mealybugs: white cottony clumps in leaf joints
Fungus gnats: small flies over damp mix
Root rot from cold, soggy mix
Bacterial or fungal leaf spot: brown, water-soaked spots
plants.pest_steps:
Check leaf undersides and leaf joints once a week, and before any plant comes indoors.
Keep newly moved plants apart from the others for 2 weeks.
Wipe leaves with a damp cloth to remove dust and mites.
For mites, thrips or mealybugs: spray insecticidal soap or neem oil every 5-7 days for three rounds. Test one leaf first and do not spray in hot sun.
For mealybugs on a few spots: touch each with a swab of 70% rubbing alcohol.
For fungus gnats: let the top inch of mix dry, add yellow sticky traps, and water once with Bti (Mosquito Bits) soaked water.
Remove leaves with leaf spot, keep the foliage dry and give the plant airflow.
plants.pests_current: No pests identified in the photos so far. Note here anything you see, with the date.
plants.growth_habit: Evergreen climbing tropical vine (an aroid) with aerial roots
plants.zone_notes: Damaged below about 50°F; a houseplant here. Grown outdoors in South Florida and Hawaii.
plants.native_range: Southern Mexico to Panama, in tropical forest.
plants.conservation_status: No IUCN Red List assessment that Claude could confirm.
plants.invasive: Not a risk in Central Texas.
plants.bloom: A cream spathe around a thick spadix, on mature plants; rare indoors.
plants.fruit: Mature plants grow a long green fruit, the "fruit salad" fruit. Fully ripe flesh is edible, tasting of pineapple and banana; unripe fruit is full of irritating crystals. Rarely forms indoors.
plants.danger_humans: All parts contain needle-like calcium oxalate crystals. Chewing them causes burning pain and swelling of the mouth, tongue and throat, drooling and trouble swallowing; the sap can irritate skin and eyes. Rarely serious, but keep it from children and wash your hands after pruning. Only fully ripe fruit is safe to eat.
plants.danger_animals: Toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA): the calcium oxalate crystals cause pawing at the mouth, drooling, mouth swelling, vomiting and trouble swallowing.
plants.propagation:
Stem cuttings with a node and an aerial root, in water, moss or moist chunky mix.
Air layering on a tall plant.
Seed, rarely available.

aliases: Possibly 'Red Peacock' or a similar speckled red cultivar
id_basis: Red-pink leaf margins and green-pink speckling are typical of red Aglaonema. Exact cultivar not determined.

Red-pink leaf margins, pink leaf stalks and heavy yellow-green and red speckling over green are typical of the red Aglaonema cultivars. The October 25 photos show the speckling clearly, which fits 'Red Peacock' and similar speckled kinds better than 'Siam Aurora', whose leaf centres are plain green. Without a tag the exact cultivar stays open.
